In this work, Yang addressed an important problem related to cross-lingual transfer learning, where the goal is to solve a natural language understanding task on a specific language, for example German, but the model only has access to supervised training data in English. Recently, pre-trained transformer models, such as multilingual BERT or XLM-RoBERTa have demonstrated surprisingly good performance, yet there is a lot of variance in performance on the target language between different fine-tuning runs. It is hard to know which model will work best, because in the zero-shot setting, you don’t have access to any labeled data in the target language. Our solution is a learned ranker that learns to predict which multilingual model will perform best on a given target language. This was found to work better than English development data, which is the standard method currently used in the literature.

Our EMNLP 2021 paper (arxiv.org/abs/2102.10242) proposes a new reinforcement learning framework – ENIGMA – for automating the Turing test. ENIGMA adopts an off-policy approach and only requires a handful of pre-collected experience data. Therefore, the evaluation does not involve human interaction with the target agent during the evaluation, making automated evaluations feasible. We believe that our proposed framework can serve as a fundamental building block to evaluation of dialogue systems and will motivate more sophisticated and stronger follow-up work on the automated Turing test.

excerpts:
EMNLP is where the evaluation and failure-mode work that enterprise NLP teams eventually depend on gets published first, usually a year or two before it reaches a vendor roadmap. The Industry Track is the part to book for: it is explicitly reserved for real deployments — latency and efficiency work, infrastructure for large-scale serving, continuous system maintenance, human-in-the-loop design, offline versus online evaluation, robustness and reliability, and ethics and bias in shipped systems. For a head of AI running retrieval, extraction, summarisation or agent systems in production, that track plus the tutorial day is a far cheaper way to pressure-test an architecture than a failed pilot, and the recruiting pool for senior NLP staff is physically in the room. Budapest also keeps European travel costs well below a US flagship conference.

## Event Features

* ✓ Main conference, 24-29 October 2026, at Hungexpo in Budapest
* ✓ 22 main-conference areas from language modelling and LLM agents through to speech and clinical NLP
* ✓ Special Theme Track: 'New Missions for NLP Research'
* ✓ Industry Track for deployed NLP systems, capped at six pages plus unlimited references and appendices
* ✓ System demonstrations track
* ✓ Tutorial programme — three-hour slots, exceptionally six hours, jointly called with AACL-IJCNLP 2026
* ✓ Co-located workshops (schedule still to be confirmed at time of writing)
* ✓ Hybrid attendance with in-person and virtual presentation options for accepted papers
* ✓ Key dates: acceptance notifications 20 August 2026, camera-ready 20 September 2026

## What Makes This Unique

* ★ One of the flagship venues in natural language processing alongside ACL and NAACL, rated top-tier (CORE A\*) — this is where the field's empirical results land first.

Where is EMNLP 2026 held?
    EMNLP 2026 is held in Budapest, Hungary. The event format is hybrid.

How much does EMNLP 2026 cost?
    EMNLP 2026 is paid. Registration rates for EMNLP 2026 are not published — the official registration page reads 'Coming soon' as of 2 August 2026, and no early-bird deadline has been announced. That is consistent with the timeline: acceptance notifications are not due until 20 August 2026 and camera-ready until 20 September, and ACL-family registration usually opens once authors know their status. Note that every accepted paper must be presented at the conference to appear in the proceedings, so at least one author registration per paper is effectively mandatory, and both in-person Budapest attendance and a virtual presentation option are offered. Host-hotel and accommodation details are also still listed as forthcoming.

# EMNLP 2024

Faculty and students presented the following papers at the Proceedings of the Ninth Conference on Machine Translation at EMNLP 2024 – Association for Computational Linguistics, held at Miami, Florida from 12 to 16 November:

* [chrF-S: Semantics Is All You Need](https://aclanthology.org/2024.wmt-1.33) – Ananya Mukherjee and Manish Shrivastava

Here is the summary of the research work:

Machine translation (MT) evaluation metrics like BLEU and chrF++ are widely used reference-based metrics that do not require training and are language-independent. However, these metrics primarily focus on n-gram matching and often overlook semantic depth and contextual understanding. To address this gap, we introduce chrF-S (Semantic chrF++), an enhanced metric that integrates sentence embeddings to evaluate translation quality more comprehensively.

...

24) – Ananya Mukherjee, Saumitra Yadav, and Manish Shrivastava

Here is the summary of the research work:

This paper presents an evaluation of 16 machine translation systems submitted to the Shared Task of the 9th Conference of Machine Translation (WMT24) for the English-Hindi (en-hi) language pair using our Complex Structures Test (CoST) suite. Aligning with this year’s test suite sub-task theme, “Help us break LLMs”, we curated a comprehensive test suite encompassing diverse datasets across various categories, including autobiography, poetry, legal, conversation, play, narration, technical, and mixed genres. Our evaluation reveals that all the systems struggle significantly with the archaic style of text like legal and technical writings or text with creative twist like conversation and poetry datasets, highlighting their weaknesses in handling complex linguistic structures and stylistic nuances inherent in these text types.
Our evaluation identifies the strengths and limitations of the submitted models, pointing to specific areas where further research and development are needed to enhance their performance.

* [A3-108 Controlling Token Generation in Low Resource Machine Translation Systems](https://aclanthology.org/2024.wmt-1.61) – Saumitra Yadav, Ananya Mukherjee, and Manish Shrivastava

Here is the summary of the research work:

Translating for languages with limited resources poses a persistent challenge due to the scarcity of high-quality training data. To enhance translation accuracy, we explored controlled generation mechanisms, focusing on the importance of control tokens. In our experiments, while training, we encoded the target sentence length as a control token to the source sentence, treating it as an additional feature for the source sentence.
